parts.problem_md: Define the term **tertiary sector.**
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> - The provision/selling of services/goods to consumers/businesses **[1 mark]**
> 
> Award 1 mark for a correct definition of tertiary sector.
> 
> Alternative acceptable answers:
> 
> - The stage of production that provides services to customers
> - The sector involved in retail, banking, transport or other service activities

> **[exam-tip]**
> Make sure you focus on the idea of providing **services** rather than manufacturing or extracting raw materials, as these relate to the secondary and primary sectors respectively. A common mistake is confusing the tertiary sector with the secondary sector — remember, tertiary is about services (e.g. banking, retail, transport), not making products.

**[1 mark]**

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> *Irsi Chocolatier* is a chocolate shop in Brussels, the capital city of Belgium. There are many other chocolate shops nearby. Opened in 1989 by the Corne family the business now has four directors and three employees. Florent Corne is the Managing Director with three other family members as Directors. *Irsi Chocolatier* opens from Tuesday till Saturday. The shop sells a variety of handmade chocolates and jelly fruit sweets. It delivers locally and has a website for information purposes only.

Which **one **of the following is the sector that converts raw materials into products?

Select **one **answer.
parts.solution_md:
**The correct answer is D**

The secondary sector converts raw materials into finished products through manufacturing or construction.

**A** is incorrect as the public sector refers to business organisations owned by the government

**B** is incorrect as the tertiary sector is the provider of services

**C** is incorrect as the primary sector is the extraction of raw materials from the earth

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> As We Grow (AWG) is a clothing business in Iceland. The social objective of the business is to use natural materials, such as wool, and produce environmentally friendly products. It aims to design clothes that will last a long time, to encourage families to buy fewer clothes and reduce waste in society.
> 
> AWG’s increasing product range now includes jumpers, dresses, shirts and baby clothes. These are produced in small workshops that employ family and friends. Waste is kept to a minimum and any leftover material is used to make scarves and hats.
> 
> The business has one store in Iceland. It uses its website to advertise and sell its clothing online to customers in other countries. The business has received the Icelandic Design Award for its contribution to the environment.

Outline why *AWG *can be classified as operating in the secondary sector.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> - AWG takes raw materials, such as wool **[1 mark]**
> - and converts them into jumpers and dresses **[1 mark]**
> 
> 1 mark for identifying a reason why AWG can be classified as operating in the secondary sector
> 
> 1 further mark for outlining the reason in the context of the business
> 
> "Outline" requires a brief description — students should identify a relevant point and develop it with context from the extract
> 
> Alternative acceptable responses include:
> 
> - AWG takes natural materials such as wool and manufactures them into clothing items like jumpers, dresses and baby clothes in its small workshops
> - Accept any appropriate response

> **[exam-tip]**
> Make sure you link your answer to the business in the extract. Simply stating that the secondary sector involves manufacturing is not enough for full marks — you need to use specific examples from the extract, such as the raw materials (e.g. wool) and the finished products (e.g. jumpers, dresses). The command word "outline" means you should give a brief but developed point, so aim to identify the reason and then add context from AWG to secure both marks.

**[2 marks]**

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> *Thornton Steel Works* is a manufacturing company based in Sheffield, England. The business was established in 2005 and employs 45 workers. It purchases iron ore and other raw materials from mining companies and transforms them into steel beams and girders used in construction. The company supplies its products to building firms across the United Kingdom. Thornton Steel Works operates from a large factory and has recently invested in new machinery to increase production capacity.

Which **one** of the following is the sector in which *Thornton Steel Works* operates?

Select **one** answer.
parts.solution_md:
**The correct answer is C**

The secondary sector involves the manufacturing or construction of goods, converting raw materials into finished or semi-finished products. Thornton Steel Works transforms iron ore into steel beams, which is a manufacturing activity.

**A** is incorrect as the tertiary sector provides services rather than manufacturing goods

**B** is incorrect as the primary sector involves the extraction of raw materials from the earth, such as mining or farming

**D** is incorrect as the quaternary sector involves knowledge-based activities such as research and development or information technology

parts.problem_md: Define the term **primary sector.**
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> - The extraction of raw materials from the earth **[1 mark]**
> 
> Award 1 mark for a correct definition of primary sector.
> 
> Alternative acceptable answer:
> 
> - The stage of production where natural resources are gathered/harvested before being processed

> **[exam-tip]**
> Make sure your definition focuses on the extraction or gathering of natural resources rather than the processing or manufacturing of goods — that would describe the secondary sector. A common mistake is to confuse the primary sector with farming alone; remember it includes all extraction of raw materials, such as mining, fishing and forestry.

**[1 mark]**

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> *NEXT *is a well-known clothing retailer that operates in 70 countries and employs over 43,000 employees. Since *NEXT *commenced trading it has introduced many other products to its range such as home interiors, flowers and a wedding list service.
> 
> In 1999 *NEXT *launched its own online shopping platform, enabling customers to purchase its products where ever they live. It continues to improve its customer service by introducing new initiatives such as next day delivery.
> 
> *NEXT *mainly uses its own factories for production. However, it does purchase some clothes such as ladies dresses from Turkish factories.

Which **one **of the following sectors would a retail outlet operate in?

Select **one **answer.
parts.solution_md:
**The correct answer is C**

A retail outlet provides a service by selling goods to customers, which places it in the tertiary sector.

**A** is incorrect as the primary sector involves extracting raw materials

**B** is incorrect as the secondary sector involves the manufacturing of goods

**D** is incorrect as the quaternary sector is not the sector in which retail operates

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> *Bright Futures Tutoring* is a private tutoring service based in Manchester, England. Founded in 2015 by Sarah Okonkwo, the business employs eight tutors who provide one-to-one and group tuition in Maths, English and Science. The company operates from a rented office but most sessions take place online or at students' homes. *Bright Futures Tutoring* also offers career advice workshops for secondary school students during the summer holidays.

Which one of the following best describes the sector in which *Bright Futures Tutoring* operates?

Select **one** answer.
parts.solution_md:
**The correct answer is C**

The tertiary sector provides services to consumers and other businesses. *Bright Futures Tutoring* provides tutoring and career advice services, placing it in the tertiary sector.

**A** is incorrect as the primary sector involves the extraction of raw materials from the earth, e.g. farming or mining

**B** is incorrect as the secondary sector converts raw materials into finished products through manufacturing or construction

**D** is incorrect as the quaternary sector focuses on knowledge-based activities such as research and development

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**

> 
> Award 1 further mark for outlining the reason in the context of the business

parts.problem_md: Define the term **secondary sector.**

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> Oakhurst is a small dairy farm in New Zealand. It sells fresh milk to local supermarkets and has recently started producing its own cheese and butter.

Explain one benefit to Oakhurst of moving from the primary sector into the secondary sector.
parts.solution_md:
Oakhurst can add value to its raw milk **[1 mark]** by turning it into cheese and butter. These processed products can be sold at a higher price **[1 mark]** than fresh milk, which could increase Oakhurst's revenue and profit margins **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Award 1 mark for identifying a benefit to Oakhurst of moving from the primary sector into the secondary sector
> 
> 2 further marks are awarded for explaining the benefit, within Oakhurst's context, for a maximum of 3 marks
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer**
> 
> - By producing cheese and butter, Oakhurst is less dependent on just selling fresh milk **[1 mark]**. This means if milk prices fall or a supermarket finds a cheaper supplier, the business has other products to rely on **[1 mark]**, reducing the risk of losing income **[1 mark]**
> - Cheese and butter have a longer shelf life than fresh milk **[1 mark]**, which spoils quickly. This means Oakhurst has more time to sell its products and is less likely to waste unsold stock **[1 mark]**, helping to reduce costs **[1 mark]**
> - Accept any other appropriate response.

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> Bloom is a flower shop in Amsterdam, Netherlands. It buys flowers from local growers and sells them directly to customers. The owner, Katja, has noticed that more customers are ordering flowers online rather than visiting the shop.

Explain one reason why a business like Bloom operates in the tertiary sector.
parts.solution_md:
Bloom does not extract or grow raw materials, nor does it manufacture products **[1 mark]**. Instead it provides the service of arranging and selling flowers **[1 mark] **to customers in Amsterdam, which is a tertiary sector activity **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Award 1 mark for identifying a reason why a business like Bloom operates in the tertiary sector
> 
> 2 further marks are awarded for explaining the benefit, within Bloom's context, for a maximum of 3 marks
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer**
> 
> - Bloom provides a service by selling flowers directly to customers rather than growing or manufacturing them **[1 mark]**. This places it in the tertiary sector because it acts as a retailer **[1 mark]**, connecting the growers who produce the flowers with the consumers who want to buy them **[1 mark]**
> - Bloom operates in the tertiary sector because it buys finished products from growers and sells them on to customers **[1 mark]**. As more customers are now ordering online, Bloom is also providing a delivery service **[1 mark]**, which is another characteristic of a tertiary sector business **[1 mark]**
> - Accept any other appropriate response.

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> Ferro is a steel manufacturer based in São Paulo, Brazil. In recent years, the Brazilian economy has shifted, and the service sector has grown significantly, while manufacturing has declined.

Explain one impact on Ferro of the economy shifting towards the tertiary sector
parts.solution_md:
Ferro may find it harder to recruit skilled workers **[1 mark] **as more people in São Paulo choose to work in the growing service sector instead. This could lead to staff shortages **[1 mark]**, making it more difficult for Ferro to maintain its production levels **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Award 1 mark for identifying an impact on Ferro of the economy shifting towards the tertiary sector
> 
> 2 further marks are awarded for explaining the benefit, within Ferrero's context, for a maximum of 3 marks
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer**
> 
> - As the service sector grows and manufacturing declines, demand for Ferro's steel may fall **[1 mark] **if fewer businesses need it for construction or production. This could lead to lower revenue **[1 mark]**, forcing Ferro to reduce output or find new markets for its products outside Brazil **[1 mark]**
> - The government in Brazil may redirect investment and support towards service sector **[1 mark]** businesses rather than manufacturers like Ferro. This could mean less funding or tax incentives available to Ferro **[1 mark]**, increasing its costs and making it harder to compete internationally **[1 mark]**
> - Accept any other appropriate response.

parts.problem_md: Explain one reason why a country's economy might shift from the primary sector to the secondary and tertiary sectors over time.
parts.solution_md:
As a country develops, wages tend to rise, making primary sector activities like farming less profitable **[1 mark]**. Businesses may move into manufacturing or services where they can add more value and generate higher returns **[1 mark]**, leading to greater economic growth **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Award 1 mark for identifying a reason why a country's economy might shift from the primary sector to the secondary and tertiary sectors over time
> 
> 2 further marks are awarded for explaining the reason, for a maximum of 3 marks
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer**
> 
> - Advances in technology **[1 mark] **can reduce the need for workers in the primary sector, as machines can do jobs like mining or harvesting more efficiently **[1 mark]**. Workers then move into the secondary and tertiary sectors, where there is greater demand for skilled labour **[1 mark]**, shifting the balance of the economy
> - As people's incomes increase, they tend to spend more on services such as healthcare, entertainment and education **[1 mark] **rather than basic raw materials. This growing demand for services encourages businesses to set up in the tertiary sector **[1 mark]**, causing the economy to shift away from the primary sector over time **[1 mark]**
> - Accept any other appropriate response.

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> Maple is a sugar cane farm in Jamaica. The owner, Devon, is considering building a small factory on site to process sugar cane into packaged sugar and rum, rather than selling the raw cane to other manufacturers.

Analyse the benefits to Maple of moving from the primary sector into the secondary sector.
parts.solution_md:
By processing sugar cane into packaged sugar and rum, Maple can add value **[1 mark] **to its raw materials and sell them at a much higher price **[1 mark]**. This would increase revenue and profit margins compared to simply selling unprocessed cane to other manufacturers, who currently capture that added value themselves **[1 mark]**

Producing its own finished products would also make Maple less dependent on other manufacturers **[1 mark]**. Currently, if a manufacturer finds a cheaper supplier of raw cane, Maple could lose income **[1 mark]**. By selling packaged sugar and rum directly, Devon would have more control over his pricing and a wider range of potential customers **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Award up to 2 marks for identifying benefits to Maple of moving from the primary sector into the secondary sector
> 
> Up to 2 further marks are awarded for applying the benefits to Maple's context
> 
> Up to 2 further marks are awarded for explaining the benefits to the business
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer**
> 
> - Manufacturing packaged sugar and rum on-site would allow Maple to diversify its product range **[1 mark]**. Instead of relying solely on selling raw sugar cane, Devon would have multiple products to sell, which spreads risk **[1 mark]** and means the business is less vulnerable if the price of raw cane falls on the global market **[1 mark]**
> - Building a factory would also create new jobs in the local area of Jamaica **[1 mark]**. This could improve Maple's reputation in the community **[1 mark]** and may attract support from the government, such as grants or tax incentives for businesses that contribute to local employment and economic development **[1 mark]**
> - Processing sugar cane into rum could allow Maple to target the tourism market in Jamaica **[1 mark]**, where demand for locally-produced rum is high. This gives Devon access to a profitable new customer base **[1 mark] **that he cannot reach by simply selling raw cane, potentially increasing sales significantly **[1 mark]**
> - Accept any other appropriate response.

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> Forge is a car parts manufacturer based in Turin, Italy. Over the past five years, several of its competitors have closed down as the Italian economy has shifted towards the service sector. Forge has seen a decline in orders from Italian carmakers, who are increasingly sourcing cheaper parts from factories in Asia.

Analyse the impacts on Forge of the Italian economy shifting towards the tertiary sector.
parts.solution_md:
As the economy shifts towards services, Forge may find it increasingly difficult to recruit skilled factory workers **[1 mark]**. Young people in Turin may prefer to train for careers in the growing service sector rather than manufacturing, leading to staff shortages **[1 mark]** that could reduce Forge's production capacity and its ability to fulfil orders **[1 mark]**

The decline in orders from Italian carmakers means Forge's revenue is likely to fall **[1 mark]**. With competitors already closing down and customers sourcing cheaper parts from Asia, Forge may struggle to cover its fixed costs **[1 mark] **such as factory rent and machinery, which could threaten the long-term survival of the business **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Award up to 2 marks for identifying impacts on Forge of the Italian economy shifting towards the tertiary sector
> 
> Up to 2 further marks are awarded for applying the impacts to Forge's context
> 
> Up to 2 further marks are awarded for explaining the impacts to the business
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer**
> 
> - The shift towards the tertiary sector may mean the Italian government focuses its support on service industries **[1 mark]** rather than manufacturing. Forge could receive less funding, fewer tax incentives or reduced infrastructure investment **[1 mark]**, increasing its operating costs at a time when it is already facing falling orders from carmakers **[1 mark]**
> - With competitors closing down, Forge may benefit from less competition in the Italian car parts market **[1 mark]**. If Forge can survive the shift, it could pick up customers from former competitors **[1 mark]**, potentially increasing its market share and strengthening its position despite the wider economic changes **[1 mark]**
> - Forge may be forced to reduce its workforce as orders decline from Italian carmakers **[1 mark]**. This would increase unemployment in Turin and could also damage staff morale among remaining employees **[1 mark]**, who may feel insecure about their jobs, leading to lower productivity **[1 mark]**
> - Accept any other appropriate response.

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> Sahara is a cotton farm in Egypt. The owner, Hassan, currently sells raw cotton to textile factories. He has noticed that the price of raw cotton has dropped significantly over the past two years due to increased competition from cheaper suppliers in India and Bangladesh.

Explain one reason why Hassan might consider moving Sahara into the secondary sector.
parts.solution_md:
Manufacturing products from his own cotton would give Hassan more control over his pricing **[1 mark]**. Currently he is dependent on factory buyers who can choose cheaper suppliers, but by selling finished goods directly he would no longer rely on these customers **[1 mark]**, reducing the risk to the business **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Award 1 mark for identifying a reason why Hassan might consider moving Sahara into the secondary sector.
> 
> 2 further marks are awarded for explaining the benefit, within Sahara's context, for a maximum of 3 marks
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer**
> 
> - Moving into the secondary sector would mean Hassan is no longer competing directly with cheaper cotton suppliers in India and Bangladesh **[1 mark]**. Instead of selling raw cotton at falling prices, he could manufacture textile products that are harder to undercut **[1 mark]**, giving Sahara a more stable source of income **[1 mark]**
> - By processing raw cotton into finished products such as fabric or clothing, Hassan could add value and charge higher prices **[1 mark]**. This would help increase revenue **[1 mark]** at a time when the falling price of raw cotton is reducing Sahara's income due to cheaper competition from India and Bangladesh **[1 mark]**
> - Accept any other appropriate response.

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> BrightPath is a private tutoring company based in Manchester. It was founded by Amara eight years ago and employs twelve tutors. BrightPath provides one-to-one and small group tutoring sessions in maths and science to secondary school students. Over the past two years, demand for in-person tutoring has fallen by 25% as families increasingly choose cheaper online tutoring platforms. Amara has £40,000 in savings.

Amara is considering two options to improve the business's financial position:

- Option 1: Remain in the tertiary sector and reduce costs by moving all tutoring sessions online, cutting the expense of renting classroom space.
- Option 2: Move into the secondary sector alongside tertiary operations by producing and selling branded revision guides and workbooks, while continuing to offer tutoring services.

Justify which one of these two options BrightPath should choose.
parts.solution_md:
The tertiary sector involves providing services to consumers and other businesses, such as tutoring. The secondary sector involves processing raw materials into finished products, such as manufacturing books **[K]**

Moving all tutoring online would reduce BrightPath's overhead costs **[K]**, as Amara would no longer need to pay rent for classroom space. This would help protect profit margins despite the 25% fall in demand for in-person tutoring **[Ap]**, without requiring Amara to develop entirely new skills or products **[An]**

However, switching entirely to online tutoring means BrightPath would be competing directly with the cheaper online platforms that are already taking its customers **[K]**. Without a clear unique selling point, BrightPath may struggle to differentiate itself in a crowded online market **[An]**. It also does not create any new revenue streams, so the business remains dependent on tutoring income alone **[Ap]**, meaning revenue may continue to decline if the trend towards cheaper alternatives continues **[An]**

Producing branded revision guides and workbooks would allow Amara to add value **[K]** by using the expertise of her twelve experienced tutors to create high-quality educational materials. These could be sold to students across the country, not just those in Manchester **[Ap]**, giving BrightPath access to a much larger market and reducing its dependence on local tutoring demand **[An]**

The drawback is that manufacturing and distributing physical products would require significant investment **[K]** from Amara's £40,000 savings **[Ap]**. If the guides do not sell well, Amara could lose most of her financial safety net, and her tutors are experienced in teaching, not writing or publishing, so developing quality materials would take time and additional resources **[An]**

BrightPath should choose Option 2 **[E]**. The decline in demand for in-person tutoring is driven by a long-term shift towards online learning, so simply cutting costs by going online is only a short-term fix that places BrightPath in direct competition with established, lower-cost platforms **[E]**. By producing its own revision guides and workbooks, BrightPath can leverage its tutors' subject expertise to create a unique product **[Ap]**, building a more diversified and sustainable business model for the future **[E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - **9-mark ‘justify’ questions are marked using a level-of-response grid (L1 - L3)**
> - Examiners judge how well the response demonstrates:
> 
>   - Accurate knowledge of relevant business concepts and terminology
>   - Application of ideas to the case study throughout the answer
>   - Logical chains of reasoning explaining business impacts
>   - A clear judgement, providing justification for the choice made
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer**
> 
> - Remaining in the tertiary sector is less risky for Amara → she has eight years of experience running a tutoring business and understands the education market well
> - Moving online keeps the business focused on what Amara knows best → rather than moving into publishing where she has no experience and could make costly mistakes
> - Manchester has a large student population and strong demand for educational support → BrightPath's local reputation could be used to market revision guides effectively
> - Revision guides branded with BrightPath's name could build trust with parents who value expert-written materials → a unique selling point that generic online platforms would be unable to match

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> Cresta is a small coffee farm in Colombia. It was set up fifteen years ago by Sofia Reyes and employs twelve workers who harvest coffee beans by hand. The beans are sold to large international companies who roast, package and sell them under their own brand names. Sofia has noticed that the price she receives for raw coffee beans has fallen steadily over the past three years, while the price of branded coffee in shops continues to rise.
> 
> Sofia has recently completed a course in coffee roasting and has saved \$40,000 from the business over the past five years. A roasting machine and packaging equipment would cost around \$35,000. Cresta has a strong reputation locally for producing high-quality beans, and Sofia has been approached by several independent cafés in Bogotá who are interested in buying locally roasted Colombian coffee.
> 
> Sofia is considering whether Cresta should move into the secondary sector by roasting and packaging its own coffee to sell directly to customers online.

Evaluate whether Cresta should move into the secondary sector by roasting and packaging its own coffee. You should use the information provided as well as your own knowledge of business.
parts.solution_md:
The secondary sector involves turning raw materials into finished products through manufacturing or processing **[K]**

Moving into the secondary sector would allow Sofia to add value **[K]** to Cresta's coffee beans by roasting and packaging them. Instead of selling raw beans at falling prices to large companies **[Ap]**, she could charge much more for a finished product **[An]**. Sofia has already been approached by independent cafés in Bogotá, so there is existing demand, and with \$40,000 in savings and equipment costing \$35,000 **[Ap]**, she has enough finance to make the investment **[An]**

However, roasting and packaging coffee requires different skills and knowledge to farming **[K]**. Although Sofia has completed a roasting course, she has no experience of running a manufacturing operation, marketing a brand or selling online **[Ap]**. Her twelve workers are skilled at harvesting, not processing, so she may need to recruit or retrain staff, which would add further costs **[An]**. With only \$5,000 left after buying equipment **[Ap]**, Cresta would have very little financial cushion if things go wrong **[An]**

Overall, Cresta should move into the secondary sector **[E]**. The price of raw beans is falling while branded coffee prices are rising **[Ap]**, meaning staying in the primary sector alone will only lead to declining income. Sofia has the savings, the training and interested buyers already in place **[Ap]**, which reduces the risk **[E]**. She could manage the transition gradually by continuing to sell raw beans to international companies while building up the roasting side of the business, rather than switching completely and risking everything at once **[E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - **12-mark 'evaluate' questions are marked using a level-of-response grid (L1 - L3)**
> - Examiners judge how well the response demonstrates:
> 
>   - Accurate knowledge of relevant business concepts and terminology
>   - Application of ideas to the case study throughout the answer
>   - Logical chains of reasoning explaining business impacts linking points together to show clear cause and effect
>   - A clear, justified conclusion based on evaluation of the issues
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer**
> 
> - Cresta already has a strong local reputation for producing high-quality beans → gives Sofia a head start in building a brand
> - Customers and cafés are increasingly interested in knowing where their coffee comes from → being able to sell Colombian-roasted coffee directly from the farm could be a powerful selling point → larger international brands cannot easily match it
> - Sofia would be competing against large international companies that already have established brands, marketing budgets and distribution networks → as a small farm with no experience of selling online, Cresta may struggle to attract enough customers beyond the few cafés in Bogotá → difficult to generate enough sales to cover the cost of the equipment and justify the move

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> Harvest is a lavender farm in the south of France. It was set up by Pierre twenty years ago and employs fifteen workers. Pierre sells his raw lavender to large cosmetics companies who use it to produce perfumes, soaps and essential oils. Over the past three years, the price Pierre receives for raw lavender has fallen by 20% due to cheaper imports from Eastern Europe. Pierre has €50,000 in savings.

Pierre is considering two options to improve the business's financial position:

- Option 1: Remain in the primary sector and reduce costs by investing in automated machinery to replace some manual labour.
- Option 2: Move into the secondary sector by building a small production unit to process lavender into essential oils and soaps, and sell them directly to tourists and local shops.

Justify which one of these two options Harvest should choose.
parts.solution_md:
The primary sector involves extracting raw materials from the earth, such as farming. The secondary sector involves processing raw materials into finished products **[K]**

Investing in automated machinery would reduce Harvest's labour costs **[K]**, as machines can work faster and longer than manual workers. This would help Pierre maintain his profit margins despite the 20% fall in the price of raw lavender **[Ap]**, without having to change the way the business operates **[An]**

However, automation would mean some of Pierre's fifteen workers could lose their jobs **[K]**. This could damage Harvest's reputation in the local community **[An]**. It also does not solve the underlying problem of falling prices caused by cheaper imports from Eastern Europe **[Ap]**, meaning revenue may continue to decline even with lower costs **[An]**

Moving into the secondary sector by producing essential oils and soaps would allow Pierre to add value **[K] **to his lavender and sell finished products at much higher prices.
